evidence_quotes.quote: This paper describes an empirical application of a strengths-based approach (SBA) to assess changes in gender equality, and draws out implications for research, evaluation, and wider development practice.

The NGO WASH programmes had incorporated gendered participatory approaches. Live and Learn Fiji had utilised “learning circles”, an inclusive, deliberative, group-based approach to dialogue and decision-making where sub-groups of youth, women, and men engaged on issues of water governance. World Vision Vanuatu’s WASH projects had utilised the WHO-UNDP Participatory Hygiene and Sanitation Transformation (PHAST) methodology with combined groups of women and men.
Two rural communities participated in Vanuatu and in Fiji, with around 15–25 women and a similar or slightly lower number of men in each site.
reveal and document the gender outcomes of the NGO programmes concerned and provide suggestions to improve practice.

criterion_notes.c1: No. Although the empirical case study is situated in communities where two NGO WASH programmes operated, the paper does not examine determinants or patterns of household or community water or sanitation service access; instead, it evaluates the methodological application of a strengths-based approach (Appreciative Inquiry) to assess changes in gender equality resulting from development initiatives (and in Fiji no WASH infrastructure was provided at all).
criterion_notes.c2: No under both readings. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the study examines NGO development project delivery, participatory behavioural/deliberative facilitation (Live and Learn Fiji 'learning circles' and World Vision Vanuatu PHAST), and an appreciative-inquiry evaluation methodology — none of which is a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism governing WASH service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs, enforcement, or utility regulation). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, although Fiji's NGO 'learning circles' touched on water governance dialogue and Vanuatu participants reported women joining community committees as a gender outcome, no legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor is examined as an exposure shaping WASH service access; hence plain_criterion2_decision is also exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. The paper reports primary empirical fieldwork from four rural case-study communities (two in Fiji and two in Vanuatu) using a sequenced participatory mixed-methods design (paired interviews, group synthesis, ranking, visioning role-plays, participatory pocket-voting quantification, and NVivo grounded-theory coding).
criterion_notes.c4: No. The study assesses changes in gender equality and gender relations (household division of labour, reduced domestic violence, respect for women, women's voice and representation on committees) and the utility of a strengths-based evaluation process. While Table 1 notes that World Vision's infrastructure project in Vanuatu reduced women's water-collection burden and satisfied practical needs for closer water and toilets, infrastructure provision is the background NGO project intervention rather than a measured service-access outcome of a legal or governance factor (and no infrastructure was provided in Fiji).
criterion_notes.c5: Yes for the authors' own research question: the rural community populations in Fiji and Vanuatu, the NGO WASH / strengths-based inquiry exposure, the gender-equality outcomes, and the participatory mixed-methods case-study design are clearly described (though an eligible legal/governance exposure and WASH service-access outcome are absent).
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is written in English (with translated abstracts in French, Spanish, and Portuguese).

study_design: Participatory mixed-methods case study informed by Appreciative Inquiry (paired/small-group interviews, sex-segregated and joint group discussions, ranking, role-play visioning, participatory pocket-voting quantification, and NVivo coding)
population_and_sample: Four rural Melanesian communities (two in Fiji and two in Vanuatu), with approximately 15–25 women and a similar or slightly lower number of men per site, plus facilitating NGO and research staff
exposure: Application of a strengths-based evaluation methodology (Appreciative Inquiry) to two NGO WASH development initiatives using gendered participatory approaches (Live and Learn Fiji 'learning circles' without infrastructure and World Vision Vanuatu PHAST plus WASH infrastructure)
outcome: Changes in gender equality and gender relations at household and community levels (e.g., respect for women, shared water-carrying labour, reduced domestic violence, women's committee participation and leadership, and reduced female labour burden from NGO WASH provision in Vanuatu), alongside methodological reflections on strengths-based approaches
rationale: Excluded as wrong topic (E01): this paper is a development-evaluation methodology and practice article assessing the merits and limitations of a strengths-based approach (Appreciative Inquiry) for evaluating and addressing changes in gender equality, illustrated through gender outcomes of two NGO WASH programmes in Fiji and Vanuatu. It does not examine determinants of household or community WASH service access (c1 = no), does not test any rule-type legal, regulatory, administrative, or governance mechanism governing service access under either the narrow 2026-10-13 reading or the plain wording of Criterion 2 (c2 = no; exposure is NGO WASH project delivery/PHAST/learning circles and SBA evaluation), and focuses on gender-relations outcomes rather than WASH service access outcomes (c4 = no).
